title: WordPress Performance Profiling with wp profile
description: A client says the site is slow. Install the WP-CLI profiler, profile the right site on a multisite network, and read the numbers before touching any code.
instructions: Type each command in the terminal below. The terminal validates your input at every step. Hints describe the action — not the exact command.

content.goal: Install wp-cli/profile-command, profile the correct site on a multisite network with an explicit --url, and read the stage table to point a client's vague "the site is slow" complaint at one concrete stage.

steps.title: 1. Install wp-cli/profile-command
paragraphs: wp profile is a separate WP-CLI package, not a core command. Install it once per environment.
On a managed host without shell package installs, this may need to be pre-approved or run locally first.

steps.title: 2. Confirm the command is available
paragraphs: wp profile --help lists the four subcommands: stage, hook, eval, eval-file.
This site is a multisite network — keep that in mind for the next step.

steps.title: 3. Profile without --url (the default mistake)
paragraphs: Running wp profile stage with no arguments profiles the network's main site — not necessarily the site anyone actually complained about.
The numbers come back looking healthy, which is the trap: they're real numbers, just for the wrong site.

steps.title: 4. Profile the actual sub-site explicitly
paragraphs: Add --url pointing at the exact sub-site from the client's complaint.
Now the template stage stands out: 0.2890s and a cache_ratio of only 61.4%, against bootstrap and main_query staying fast and well-cached.

steps.title: 5. Trim the output to what goes in the report
paragraphs: --fields keeps the table to stage, time, and cache_ratio — the three numbers worth quoting back to the client or a teammate.
From here, the next step is drilling into the template stage's hooks — covered in the next article in this series.

troubleshooting: Running wp profile stage without --url on a multisite network — it profiles the network's main site, not the sub-site anyone reported as slow.
Treating a healthy-looking wp profile stage result as proof nothing is wrong — it may just be the wrong site.
Skipping wp profile --help after install — on some hosts the package installs but the binary isn't on PATH for the web user, only for SSH.
Reading time alone and ignoring cache_ratio — a slow stage with a low cache_ratio points at uncached queries, not raw PHP execution.
Profiling once and calling it done — stage numbers vary run to run; profile 2-3 times before quoting a number to a client.

faq.question: Why does wp profile stage need --url on a multisite network?
faq.answer: Without --url, WP-CLI bootstraps the network's main site. On multisite, every sub-site can have different active plugins and theme setups, so profiling the wrong URL gives real but irrelevant numbers.

faq.question: What does a low cache_ratio actually mean?
faq.answer: It means a large share of that stage's queries went straight to the database instead of the object cache — a common cause of slow template stages, and usually the next place to investigate, not the PHP code itself.

faq.question: Is one wp profile stage run enough to diagnose a slow site?
faq.answer: No. Run it 2-3 times — caching, cron, and background jobs can make a single run look better or worse than the site's normal behavior.

faq.question: What's the difference between wp profile stage and wp profile hook?
faq.answer: wp profile stage measures WordPress's three broad load phases. wp profile hook goes one level deeper, breaking down time spent inside a specific hook's callbacks — the next step once a stage is confirmed slow.
